list.listitem: Consider a diagnosis of onychomycosis when evaluating dystrophic nails characterized by hypertrophy (thickening), discoloration, onycholysis (nail plate and bed separation), and subungual debris in a patient with tinea pedis. C
Clinical symptoms can be confirmed by histology of the nail plate using Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, potassium hydroxide (KOH) stain, or fungal culture to determine the causative organism. B

For clinical and mycological cure, the two most effective treatment options for toenail onychomycosis include oral terbinafine 250 mg daily and oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 12 to 24 weeks; adverse events appear similar. A
Topical monotherapy has been recommended when less than 50% of the nail plate is affected without nail matrix involvement, but efficacy is poor. B
Long-term cure can be expected in less than half of patients treated for toenail fungus. B

background.definition: The main subtypes of fungal infection that affect the nails include are distal lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO; the most common), white superficial onychomycosis (WSO), proximal subungual onychomycosis (PSO), endonyx onychomycosis (EO), and total dystrophic onychomycosis (TDO).

list.listitem: United States and Finland: 7% to 10%.
North American children younger than 18 years: 0.44%.
Dermatophytes, nondermatophytes (including Candida sp.), and yeast.
Trichophyton rubrum causes 80% of dermatophyte nail infections and 45% of all nail infections.
Other dermatophytes: Microsporum canis and other species, Epidermophyton floccosum and other species.

Depends on the clinical subtype. DLSO: Primary infection of underside of the nail, secondary nail bed, and hyponychium involvement. WSO: Surface of the nail first infected. PSO: Fungi primarily invade the cuticle and proximal nailfold. EO: Infection of the nail plate with no evident nail bed involvement. TDO: Advanced infection with deformation/destruction of entire nail plate. Candidal infection: Typically onycholysis, paronychia (inflammation of the nailfold).
Dermatophytes are the most common cause of onychomycosis. C
Tinea pedis in the preceding year, abnormal opaque thick nails with hyperkeratosis, and white crumbly or yellowish or brownish areas on the nail surface suggest onychomycosis. C

To rule in onychomycosis, consider PAS stain, KOH stain, or fungal culture. They have similar positive predictive values (90%, 88%, and 90%, respectively). The one advantage of fungal culture is it can identify the pathogenic organism, however, the result takes 4 weeks to come back. B

To rule out onychomycosis, send sufficient nail clippings and subungual debris on a formalin container and request PAS stain by a trained pathologist. It has the highest sensitivity (92%), highest negative predictive value (77%), and best negative likelihood ratio (0.11), compared to KOH stain and fungal culture. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Nail plate colored green or black
Oil stains, pitting, psoriatic plaques typically distributed on elbows and knees
Characterized by polygonal violaceous papules on distal extremities
Characterized by cutaneous erythema and scaling coexistent with hypertrophic nails
Longitudinal nail ridges, red and white lines, and V-shaped nicking
Dark pigmentation of 1 nail, with or without pigmentation spreading to adjacent skin (Hutchinson's sign)
Multiple nails with similar changes—stripes, shedding, discoloration
Tetracycline gives distal onycholysis with sun exposure in some patients

list.listitem: Onychomycosis is usually asymptomatic, although sometimes discomfort is reported.
Ask about environmental (sport clubs) and occupational (baker) risk factors.

Tinea pedis in preceding year increases the probability of onychomycosis. Abnormal opaque thick nails with hyperkeratosis, white crumbly or yellowish or brownish areas on nail surface also suggest onychomycosis.
Probable diagnosis of onychomysis by a dermatologist, together with plantar desquamation affecting 25% of the sole, has a positive predictive value of 81%.
Candidiasis is more frequent in fingernails than in toenails.
Direct microscopy of nail scrapings with % potassium hydroxide (KOH) in dimethylsulfoxide can visualize hyphae.
Fungal culture can identify the species of causative pathogen and can guide therapy.

Histologic examination of nail clippings with PAS stain is the most sensitive test and is useful if initial tests are negative and you still suspect the diagnosis is onychomycosis. Send to pathology in formalin.
In experienced hands, confocal microscopy may be faster and more accurate than microscopy with KOH preparations.
Suspect onychomycosis in patients with chronic nail abnormalities (eg, color changes, increased thickness, various deformities, and crumbling nails).

Initial diagnostic testing consists of direct microscopy with KOH of nail clippings, PAS stain, or fungal culture. All three tests have similar positive predictive values (88%, 90%, 90%, respectively) and are good at ruling in the diagnosis, especially when pretest probability of onychomycosis is high.

PAS stain is helpful when KOH or fungal culture is negative but onychomycosis is still suspected. PAS stain has high sensitivity (92%), good negative predictive value (77%), and very good -LR (0.11). PAS stain excels in ruling out onychomycosis. On the other hand, fungal culture has the highest false-negative rate among the 3 tests, and is least helpful in ruling out onychomycosis.

For clinical and mycological cure, the two most effective treament options for toenail onychomycosis include oral terbinafine 250 mg daily and oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 12 to 24 weeks; adverse events appear similar. A
Topical monotherapy may be considered when less than 50% of the nail plate is affected without nail matrix involvement, but overall efficacy is poor. B

Topical therapy (ciclopirox 8% lacquer or amorolfine 5% lacquer) may be considered when less than 50% of the nail is involved and the matrix is not involved. It is also an option for superficial white onychomycosis.
Two RCTs using topical ciclopirox found mycologic cure rates of 32% versus 10% with placebo (NNT = 5), but clear nails and clinical cure in only 7% versus 0.4% (NNT = 15).

A Cochrane review of 6 RCTs evaluating the topical treatment of onychomycosis concluded that topical ciclopiroxolamine has poor cure rates and that amorolfine might be substantially more effective but more research is required. Otherwise, systemic therapy is recommended (see ).

Compared with placebo, high-quality evidence supports the efficacy of topical efinaconazole 10%, while moderate-quality evidence supports the effectiveness of topical tavaborole 5% and ciclopirox 8% for the complete cure of onychomycosis. Based on very low-quality evidence, the efficacy of topical luliconazole 5% is uncertain. High to moderate-quality evidence suggests that topical efinaconazole and tavaborole causes more adverse events than placebo, while low-quality evidence suggests higher adverse events from topical ciclopirox than placebo.

An RCT of 365 patients found topical terbinafine 10% was better than placebo in treating mild to moderate distal and lateral onychomycosis affecting 20-60% of at least 1 great toenail. Complete cure rate for topical terbinafine was 4.5%, while placebo was 0%.

Despite their relative efficacy against placebo, topical therapies have low complete cure rates: efinaconazole (15.2%-17.8%), tavaborole (6.5%-9.1%). Complete cure rate is defined as clinical and mycologic cure.
Another challenge with topical therapies is the need to apply them daily for at least 48 weeks, based on most clinical trials.

A network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs evaluating topical and systemic monotherapy for toenail onychomycosis found the highest clinical and mycological cure rates with oral terbinafine 250 mg daily and oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 12 to 24 weeks. Adverse events were similar between the medications that were evaluated (ie, oral terbinafine, itraconazole, fluconazole, and topical ciclopirox 8%, efinaconazole 10%, and tavaborole 5%). Itraconazole had the best safety profile.

A network meta-analysis of systemic monotherapies for onychomycosis found that terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks, followed by a 12-week period of no therapy, and then another 4 weeks of terbinafine 250 mg daily had the highest complete cure rate at 1 year (surface under the cumulative ranking curve or SUCRA = 82.7%). This regimen showed the best balance between efficacy, safety and cost. The highest mycological cure rate was from terbinafine 250 mg daily for 24 weeks (SUCRA = 92.4%).

A systematic review found that of 100 patients treated with systemic therapy, approximately 40 patients will have normal nails 1 year later, and only 33 patients will have normal nails 2 years later. The recommended dose of oral terbinafine is 250 mg daily for 6 weeks for fingernails and 12 weeks for toenails.

Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 12 weeks or pulse therapy (200 mg twice daily for 1 of every 4 weeks for 12 weeks) is effective for toenail onychomycosis. Although based on data from network meta-analysis, continuous therapy appears more effective than pulse therapy.

Fluconazole 300 mg once weekly for 6 months was somewhat effective in a RCT with 362 patients (28%-36% clinical cure vs 3% with placebo; NNT = 3). A recent review recommended fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months.

In cases of treatment failure, consider an alternative drug or nail removal combined with further treatment during nail regrowth. The risks of nail removal in patients with comorbidities (eg, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, immunosuppression), along with high recurrence rate of onychomycosis, need to be balanced with potential benefits of complete cure.
Consider monitoring liver function tests in patients given oral antifungal agents. Recommendations vary by agent and patient. There is no evidence to guide choice of monitoring intervals.

A decision analysis study in 2016 conducted in the U.S. concluded that the most cost-effective treatment strategy for onychomycosis is empiric treatment with oral terbinafine without diagnostic confirmation of fungal infection or monitoring of liver function tests.
Based on Canadian cost of drugs, tests, and other factors, confirmatory testing before treatment has been recommended.
Patients with HIV may have severe onychomycosis and require more aggressive treatment.
Consider removal of the infected nail in patients with very thick, distorted nails.
Matrixectomy can be performed by physical or chemical means (40%-50% urea).
In one small RCT, nail debridement plus application of topical antifungal nail lacquer was more effective than nail debridement alone in improving symptoms and of mycological cure.

There is currently insufficient evidence to show effective treatment of toenail onychomycosis with lasers (eg, Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser). In one study, 51 patients were randomized to laser vs sham laser and no laser treated patients reached the primary outcome of complete clearance at 52 weeks. A Cochrane review, based on very low-quality evidence from 3 trials with 112 participants, concluded that the efficacy of 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser is uncertain.
Although a number of herbal and alternative therapies have been proposed, such as vinegar, tea tree oil, bleach, and Vick's VapoRub, they are not supported by good evidence.

One small RCT, found a nail lacquer solution containing Ageratina (snakeroot) pichinchensis to be equally clinically effective as 8% ciclopirox nail lacquer (71.1% vs 80.9%) with similar mycological cure rates (59.1% vs 63.8%). These numbers, however, are substantially higher than found in other trials of ciclopirox.
Untreated disease does not generally resolve; it slowly progresses to involve a greater proportion of the affected nail and adjacent nails. C
Expected initial cure rates with systemic treatment are 80% for fingernails and 70% for toenails. Long-term cure rates are worse, as low as 33%. B

A retrospective review of 4985 adults and children with a mean age of 43 years with 4309 courses of terbinafine and 793 courses of griseofulvin showed rates of abnormal AST or ALT either at baseline (as recommended for terbinafine) or during drug monitoring (often done at 1 month) at around 3%. Less than 0.2% of these were grade 2 or worse elevations (>3 times the upper limit). B
Although the nails may begin to improve in the first months of treatment, it may take 10 months to see clear toenails even when the treatment is a complete success.
Use protective footwear in public showers.
Treat tinea pedis immediately as it may prevent reinfection of the nails.
There is no evidence that folk remedies such as vinegar, bleach, or Vick's VapoRub are effective.
Onychomycosis is more common in older patients.
Beware of drug interactions that can occur with systemic antifungal agents.
Waiting until after pregnancy to treat onychomycosis is the safest option.
If treatment is pursued, topical therapies should be the primary treatment modality.
Exposure to itraconazole in the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with increased risk of fetal loss.
Terbinafine is the only systemic drug that is pregnancy category B; the others are category C or worse.
Check for onychomycosis in family members.
High treatment failure rate may be due to an adherence problem.
See for dosing of systemic agents in children.
